{
  "cards": [
    {
      "title": "Write Ads to Trigger the Life-Force 8 Biological Desires",
      "summary": "Anchor product messaging to one of eight hardwired human desires that drive the majority of purchasing decisions.",
      "use_when": "Choosing the core angle for a PDP headline, ad creative or launch campaign when deciding which emotional benefit to lead with.",
      "steps": [
        "Reference the Life-Force 8: (1) survival/life enjoyment/life extension, (2) enjoyment of food and beverages, (3) freedom from fear, pain and danger, (4) sexual companionship, (5) comfortable living conditions, (6) to be superior/winning/keeping up with the Joneses, (7) care and protection of loved ones, (8) social approval.",
        "Pick the single LF8 desire your product most credibly satisfies, then make that the dominant appeal across headline, hero image and first lines of body copy.",
        "Treat the nine learned/secondary wants (be informed, curiosity, cleanliness, efficiency, convenience, dependability/quality, beauty and style, economy/profit, bargains) as supporting, not leading, arguments\u2014the source argues they are far weaker because they are learned, not hardwired.",
        "Test which LF8 angle your buyers respond to (see the Haldeman-Julius example: the same book retitled 'Quest for a Blonde Mistress' jumped from 5,000 to 50,000 copies, and 'How to Argue Logically' tripled sales) by running the same product under different LF8-framed headlines and comparing click-through and purchase conversion."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "The book-title lift figures are a 1920s mail-order example, not a modern ecommerce benchmark.",
        "Pick the desire your product genuinely satisfies\u2014the source warns that appeals your product cannot deliver will fail."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "customer-research",
        "offer-design",
        "creative-strategy",
        "positioning",
        "copywriting"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Use 'Mental Movies' to Make Prospects Visualize Using the Product",
      "title": "Direct Mental Movies With Specific Visual Words",
      "summary": "Replace vague benefit claims with specific visual language that makes prospects mentally simulate using the product.",
      "use_when": "Writing product descriptions, ad body copy, landing page sections or video scripts where a generic benefit statement is falling flat.",
      "steps": [
        "Start from a vague line ('Go somewhere and do something') and progressively add specificity: location, object, action, then sensory detail (the source's progression: go to the kitchen / open the oven / pull out the pizza / pull out the freshest, crispiest pizza you've ever eaten).",
        "Use action verbs and concrete nouns so readers picture themselves performing steps with the product, not just reading a claim.",
        "Add 'positive visual adjectives' (PVAs) sparingly at key moments to intensify the image.",
        "Apply this to ecommerce PDPs: instead of 'high-quality nonstick pan', write copy that walks the buyer through the first meal they'll cook in it.",
        "For video ads, script the sequence of images the viewer should see in their mind rather than listing features; the source's framing is that 'the first use of any product is inside the consumers' minds'."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "Whitman's claim that imagery increases desire is a persuasion principle, not a measured conversion lift\u2014test copy variants against your own baseline.",
        "Overwriting dense imagery can hurt readability; the source also recommends clear readability formulas and simplicity."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "product-page",
        "creative-strategy",
        "landing-page",
        "copywriting",
        "video-ads"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Sell Benefits, Not Features, in Every Asset",
      "title": "Lead With 'What's In It For Me?' Benefits",
      "summary": "Consumers care about what the product does for them, not company facts, equipment or process.",
      "use_when": "Reviewing product pages, about sections, ad copy or brochures that currently describe the company, factory or product specs.",
      "steps": [
        "Audit each asset for self-serving content: company history, staff counts, square footage, equipment photos, 'unusual camera angles'. The source cites Daniel Starch's research showing readers ignore factory-focused ads.",
        "For each feature listed, write the corresponding consumer benefit and lead with the benefit.",
        "Put the single biggest benefit in the headline.",
        "Batch benefits throughout ('Bombard Your Readers With Benefits') rather than relying on one strong claim.",
        "Use the Flesch readability ease concept and clear layout so benefit statements land fast."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "This is the book's core 'advertising should move people to act' doctrine\u2014it is a direct-response stance, not a brand-awareness stance; brand campaigns may weight emotion and imagery differently."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "product-page",
        "positioning",
        "copywriting",
        "landing-page"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Use the Four-Part Fear Appeal (Only When You Have the Solution)",
      "title": "Build Fear Appeals With All Four Required Components",
      "summary": "Fear only converts when it is strong, paired with a specific effective solution, and the prospect believes they can act.",
      "use_when": "Writing ad copy or a landing page for a protective or problem-solving product (security, insurance, hygiene, safety gear, health supplements).",
      "steps": [
        "Confirm your product genuinely resolves the fear; if it doesn't, the source says the appeal will fail.",
        "Include all four elements (Pratkanis & Aronson, Age of Propaganda): (1) scare the prospect, (2) offer a specific recommendation to overcome the threat, (3) make the action seem effective, (4) make the prospect believe they can perform it.",
        "Target existing, widely recognized fears rather than inventing new ones\u2014e.g., sun damage sells sunscreen; UV damage to laundry does not sell detergent.",
        "Support the solution with credibility boosters: testimonials, demos, free trials.",
        "Use deadlines and scarcity ('limited offer', 'while supplies last') as a fear-of-loss variant, but still provide the clear path to buy."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "Too much fear can paralyze rather than motivate (the source's 'deer in headlights' analogy).",
        "The source explicitly ties ethical use to having a truly effective solution."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "creative-strategy",
        "copywriting",
        "landing-page",
        "scarcity",
        "positioning"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Frame Products as Identity and Ego Signals",
      "title": "Use Ego Morphing to Sell Identity, Not Just Function",
      "summary": "Present imagery and social proof that lets buyers see themselves as the kind of person who owns the product.",
      "use_when": "Merchandising lifestyle, luxury, apparel, beauty or status-adjacent products where functional copy underperforms.",
      "steps": [
        "Identify the desirable characteristic society associates with the product: physical attractiveness, intelligence, economic success, sexual prowess.",
        "Show imagery of aspirational customers\u2014per the source, perfume ads show attractive models who never even wear the product.",
        "For stores without celebrity customers, create association: the book's example suggests giving free product to recognizable local figures, then referencing who uses your service.",
        "Apply the social-proof version for B2B/service contexts: name the most rigorous clients ('why local bank presidents choose us') to transfer credibility to the average buyer.",
        "Avoid heavy persuasion copy in these assets; let the image do the ego work."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "This mostly applies to goods whose value is largely symbolic; commodity purchases usually need functional benefit copy.",
        "False or misleading customer references would be deceptive\u2014only state genuine relationships."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "creative-strategy",
        "positioning",
        "merchandising",
        "social-proof"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Write Fear Appeals Around Recognized Problems",
      "title": "Pair the Scare With a Credible, Easy Solution",
      "summary": "Fear appeals must translate into a believable, achievable action or they create inaction.",
      "use_when": "Designing acquisition creative for problem-solution products like sanitizers, supplements, insurance or safety items.",
      "steps": [
        "Diagnose your market's preexisting anxieties: for hand sanitizer, the source shows GOJO used surveys about unwashed hands and dirty money to make bacteria a foreground concern.",
        "Lead with concrete facts about the risk, then present your product as the accessible fix (the source notes Purell's travel bottles made the solution easy).",
        "For product pages, add a clear call to action with a low barrier (free shipping, sample, easy return).",
        "Use deadline mechanics\u2014'one-day sale', 'while supplies last'\u2014to nudge action on the fear of missing out.",
        "Validate the fear's credibility by targeting existing, widely-recognized fears rather than fringe concerns."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "The book's sanitizer and mint ads are historical examples of positioning, not proof of your product's efficacy.",
        "Exaggerated health or safety claims can breach advertising standards; keep claims substantiated."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "creative-strategy",
        "landing-page",
        "copywriting",
        "scarcity",
        "positioning"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Put the Biggest Benefit in the Headline and Use Headline Starters",
      "title": "Use Psychologically Potent Headlines to Stop the Scroll",
      "summary": "The headline is the highest-leverage copy element; use proven starters and lead with the strongest benefit.",
      "use_when": "Running paid social or display ads, writing email subject lines, or title-tagging a PDP or landing page.",
      "steps": [
        "Write multiple candidate headlines around one dominant benefit, not a feature or product name.",
        "Use the book's 22 headline-starter patterns (e.g., 'How to...', 'Who else...', question style) and question headlines, which the source lists as a separate power technique.",
        "Include extreme specificity numbers where honest, per 'Crush Your Competition With Extreme Specificity'.",
        "Add 'grabbers' above or before the headline (the source lists '12 ways to lure readers into your copy').",
        "Test headlines as the primary variable; the source treats the headline as the biggest determining factor of whether copy gets read."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "The '22 starters' are lists of formulas, not validated lifts; run A/B tests against your own audience.",
        "Some patterns like rhetorical questions can fail for certain products or audiences."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "creative-strategy",
        "landing-page",
        "product-page",
        "copywriting",
        "subject-lines"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Kill Human Inertia With Urgency, Guarantees and Friction Reduction",
      "title": "Battle Human Inertia at the Point of Decision",
      "summary": "Even a convinced buyer needs reasons to act now and an easy path to purchase.",
      "use_when": "Optimizing checkout, cart recovery, subscription sign-up or any step where visitors have interest but don't convert.",
      "steps": [
        "Add scarcity and deadlines to the offer: the source says fear of missing out (tied to the 'bargain' secondary want) pushes action.",
        "Write a guarantee that reduces perceived risk ('Guarantees that Guarantee Higher Response').",
        "Make buying frictionless: the source's hot lists include '13 Ways to Make Buying Easy'.",
        "Use coupon offers and coupon-style CTAs ('The Coupon Persuader') where the audience is deal-motivated.",
        "Avoid purely clever or entertaining copy that produces 'wow' reactions and zero action\u2014measure purchase conversion, not likes or comments."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "Fake scarcity or artificial deadlines are deceptive and can backfire; the source ties deadlines to a real bargain.",
        "Guarantees must match what your operations can actually honor."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "checkout",
        "conversion-optimization",
        "scarcity",
        "guarantees",
        "retention"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Use Social Proof and Authority to Build Credibility",
      "title": "Borrow Credibility Through Social Proof and Authority",
      "summary": "Prospects need to believe your claims before they buy; transfer credibility via testimonials, transfer and authority positioning.",
      "use_when": "Adding trust elements to a PDP, landing page, sales letter or paid ad for a product with a skeptical or high-consideration audience.",
      "steps": [
        "Use social proof: customer testimonials, user counts, reviews, and named companies that use the product (" +
          "the book's 'Transfer\u2014Credibility by Osmosis' and 'The Bandwagon Effect' principles).",
        "Position yourself as an authority ('Authority Positioning' technique), for example by citing credentials or specialized experience.",
        "Use 'examples vs. statistics': testimonials often beat bare statistics for emotional credibility, while stats support the rational case; the source lists both as principles #12 and #16.",
        "Reinforce with 'The Inoculation Theory' in competitive markets: mention and defuse objections before the buyer reaches checkout.",
        "For B2B or premium products, cite specific expert or peer groups ('why these types of buyers choose us')."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "Never fabricate reviews, testimonials or endorsements\u2014this is deceptive and illegal in most jurisdictions.",
        "Video and screenshot proof often work better than text claims, but require real customers."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "social-proof",
        "product-page",
        "landing-page",
        "positioning",
        "trust"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Organize the Message for Clarity and Use Repetition",
      "title": "Structure Copy for Clarity and Reinforce Key Points",
      "summary": "Message clarity and repetition are separate, stackable persuasive techniques.",
      "use_when": "Editing long-form sales pages, email sequences, or any asset that feels scattered or unclear after the first draft.",
      "steps": [
        "Apply 'Message Organization'\u2014structure with a clear single main claim, then supporting benefits in logical order (the book's AIDA framing: attention, interest, desire, action).",
        "Use 'Repetition and Redundancy' to restate key claims and the offer at multiple points; the source includes the P.S. line as a restatement of the offer, often read first.",
        "Use rhetorical questions sparingly to draw readers in and prompt agreement.",
        "Apply the Elaboration Likelihood Model concept: decide whether the audience will process carefully (give strong arguments) or lightly (favor simple, familiar cues like count of reviews or brand familiarity).",
        "Use 'message sidedness' knowingly\u2014two-sided presentations can build credibility with skeptical audiences; one-sided may work for already-persuaded buyers."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "Repetition beyond a point becomes noise; monitor engagement metrics for fatigue.",
        "Two-sided messaging is a situational choice, not a universal rule."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "copywriting",
        "landing-page",
        "conversion-optimization",
        "email-marketing",
        "repetition"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Segment Buyers With the Transtheoretical and Means-End Models",
      "title": "Match Copy to the Buyer's Stage and End Goal",
      "summary": "Persuasion step-by-step (Transtheoretical Model) and means-end chaining help you align message with where the buyer is and what they're really after.",
      "use_when": "Planning email sequences, retargeting ads or content marketing where different segments need different messages.",
      "steps": [
        "Map buyers to Transtheoretical stages \u2014 precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance \u2014 and change the CTA per stage: educational content to cold audiences, use-case demos and offers to warm, urgency and discounts to hot.",
        "Apply the Means-End Chain: link product attributes \u2192 functional benefits \u2192 emotional end states; write copy that connects the product's most concrete attribute to a specific life outcome the buyer values.",
        "For replenishment or subscription, use 'maintenance' framing: reminders, auto-refill, program benefits.",
        "Test whether different segments respond to pain-avoidance or aspiration framing (fear vs. ego)."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "The book presents these as frameworks based on academic persuasion research; there are no ecommerce lift numbers cited.",
        "Stage bands are conceptual, not numeric thresholds\u2014avoid assuming specific conversion rates."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "customer-research",
        "retention",
        "subscriptions",
        "email-marketing",
        "segmentation"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Design for Simplicity, Positioning and Readability",
      "title": "Apply Layout, Type and Color to Increase Readership",
      "summary": "Formatting choices affect how many people actually read and act on your ad.",
      "use_when": "Laying out a PDP, landing page, email or ad creative where copy is already strong but engagement is low.",
      "steps": [
        "Prioritize 'The Psychology of Simplicity' and clean layout; avoid cluttered, clever, or self-referential design.",
        "Place the strongest benefit visually prominent above the fold; apply 'The Psychology of Page and Section Positioning'.",
        "Watch the 'Reverse-Type Pitfall' \u2014 low-contrast reversed text can cut readability.",
        "Use the source's typeface and size psychology for scannability; avoid decorative fonts for body copy.",
        "Wrap ads in white space ('Wrap Your Ads in White') and use color per the source's consumer color preferences chapter, testing your own palette where possible."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "Color preference research predates current display contexts and can vary by audience; treat as guidance only.",
        "The book's design rules are based on print-era observations; mobile rendering changes some assumptions."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "product-page",
        "landing-page",
        "conversion-optimization",
        "design",
        "readability"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Insist on Specificity and the Ogilvy Principle",
      "title": "Use Specificity and the Ogilvy Principle to Stand Out",
      "summary": "Extreme specificity and following Ogilvy's evidence-based principles set your copy apart from vague competitor claims.",
      "use_when": "Writing or editing any claim in a product description, ad or landing page that currently reads generically.",
      "steps": [
        "Replace vague adjectives ('high quality', 'great value') with precise numbers, materials or outcomes\u2014the source calls this 'Crush Your Competition With Extreme Specificity'.",
        "Apply the 'Famous Ogilvy Principle' \u2014 study what the master copywriter concluded about headlines, body copy, and long vs. short content, rather than assuming shorter is always better.",
        "Match 'Long Copy vs. Short' to the buying context: high-consideration and expensive products often justify long copy; impulse and low-cost products often do not.",
        "Use the 'Unique Selling Proposition' tool \u2014 articulate a specific benefit no competitor can match and repeat it consistently.",
        "Fill product pages with concrete detail (exact dimensions, materials, ingredient sources) to signal credibility."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "Specificity must be true; unverifiable claims invite refunds and platform penalties.",
        "Optimal copy length is audience- and offer-dependent; test on your own traffic."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "copywriting",
        "product-page",
        "positioning",
        "usp",
        "conversion-optimization"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Run Offer and Copy Tests, Not Just Belief",
      "title": "Test Offers Like a Direct-Response Marketer",
      "summary": "Treat the offer, not the copy alone, as the primary testable variable.",
      "use_when": "Structuring an A/B testing roadmap for an ecommerce store's landing pages, PDPs or email campaigns.",
      "steps": [
        "Follow 'Offer Testing' as a distinct step before obsessing over copy or creative\u2014the source positions the offer as foundational to response.",
        "Use 'Survey Power' and 'A Sales Letter in Survey's Clothing' to research what buyers actually want, and to disguise research as editorial content when appropriate.",
        "Vary one element at a time and register actual response (purchase conversion), not just engagement.",
        "Add 'Editorial Energizers' \u2014 sidebars, call-outs, and pull quotes \u2014 to increase readership of the offer.",
        "Track coupon-style redemptions and multi-page vs. single-page formats where applicable."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "The source's '100 secrets' include many pre-digital tactics; adapt them to current platforms and verify how each interface works before implementing.",
        "Sample sizes on small stores make many tests statistically underpowered."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "experiment-design",
        "conversion-optimization",
        "offer-design",
        "customer-research",
        "measurement"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Ensure You Can Measure Response at All",
      "title": "Prioritize Metrics That Reflect Action, Not Applause",
      "summary": "Advertising's purpose is to make people act; measure purchases, not entertainment value.",
      "use_when": "Setting up dashboards, reviewing a campaign's results, or justifying budget for a direct-response creative project.",
      "steps": [
        "Define the target action for each asset: order, signup, quote request, or email opt-in.",
        "Reject primary KPIs like 'Wow, great ad!' reactions, likes, or shares as proxies for sales.",
        "Instrument the path from ad to purchase (link tracking, coupon codes, UTM parameters) so purchase conversion is attributable.",
        "Treat copy and creative as tools to remove friction and provide a reason to act now, not to entertain.",
        "When comparing variations, judge them on the target action, not aesthetic preference."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "Some long-cycle or high-consideration products won't show immediate purchase conversion from paid traffic; measure assisted conversions and pipeline, not only last-click."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "measurement",
        "analytics",
        "conversion-optimization",
        "attribution"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Run a Killer Ad Checklist Before Every Launch",
      "title": "Use the 46-Point Killer Ad Checklist to Review Assets",
      "summary": "A pre-launch checklist catches weak headlines, missing benefits, unclear offers and friction before spend.",
      "use_when": "Reviewing a landing page, PDP, paid ad or email before it goes live.",
      "steps": [
        "Pull the book's checklist categories: response superchargers, ways to convey value, ways to make buying easy, ways to boost coupon returns.",
        "Check for headline strength (biggest benefit), clear single proposition, and specific support.",
        "Check for urgency or deadline with a credible reason.",
        "Check for an obvious, low-friction path to purchase (clear CTA, visible price, no unexpected steps).",
        "Check for credibility signals (testimonials, guarantees, named proof).",
        "Apply 'Give Yourself a Cleverectomy' \u2014 strip clever lines that don't drive action."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "The checklist is drawn from print-era direct response; add modern essentials (mobile layout, page speed, trust badges, PCI compliance) it doesn't cover."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "checklist",
        "conversion-optimization",
        "product-page",
        "landing-page",
        "quality-assurance"
      ]
    },
    {
      "card_title": "Use the P.S. and Repetition to Restate the Offer",
      "title": "Close With a Restated Offer (The P.S. Principle)",
      "summary": "The P.S. is often read first; use it to restate the offer and push action.",
      "use_when": "Writing sales emails, sales pages or direct-mail-style landing page copy.",
      "steps": [
        "Place an offer-restating P.S. at the end of every email and long-form sales page.",
        "Repeat the offer and contact/CTA in the P.S.; the source emphasizes restating terms, price and action step.",
        "For email, mirror this with a short postscript after the signature line containing the primary CTA link.",
        "Use the same technique in ad captions and post-scripts for any long-form content."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "In modern short-form social ads, there is rarely a place for a formal P.S.; prioritize the primary CTA instead."
      ],
      "tags": [
        "ad-copy-deployment",
        "email-marketing",
        "copywriting",
        "landing-page",
        "conversion-optimization"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

The core principle of direct-response copywriting: focusing exclusively on consumer benefits ("What's In It For Me?") rather than product features.

It’s perfectly safe—that is, if she doesn’t step off the edge! One wrong step and she’d snap her neck like an old-west bandit swinging from branches of the hangman’s tree. The solution? Call Vanity ’n‘ Fur groomers, where we use loving kindness to beautify your doggie, never dangerous mechanical contraptions—like the groomer’s noose—that less-experienced groomers risk using everyday. Bottom line: Fear sells. It motivates. It urges. It moves people to action. It drives them to spend money. In fact, social psychologists and consumer researchers have been studying its effects for more than 50 years. Whether it’s selling a loaf of bread, which hardly seems scary (until you show them studies reporting that refined white flour may cause cancer), or painting a picture of doom and gloom about the insidious nature of odorless carbon monoxide creeping through air conditioning vents and wiping out their family (while they’re sleeping safely in a hotel on a business trip), properly constructed, fear can move people to spend. But why does it work? In a word: stress. Fear causes stress. And stress causes the desire to do something. Missing a big sale causes the stress of loss. Choosing the right tires can cause the stress of concern for personal safety. Not opting for the side-curtain airbags in your new car causes the stress of future regret and visions of physical injury. Fear suggests loss. Fear paints a picture of necessary response. It tells your prospect that he or she will be somehow damaged. This threatens the ego’s continuous quest for self-preservation. Therefore, the threat of being damaged is insidious and powerful. Can you use it for your products and services? Yes...if your product offers the appropriate solution for a fearful situation. But is it ethical? How to Get Inside Their Heads 31 Yes, but only if what you’re selling offers a truly effective solution. Certain products can quell fears. And there’s nothing wrong with promoting—and profiting—from them. “Oh, Drew...that’s so manipulative! Scaring people to buy! How could you?” If you thought or said this statement, please read my Introduction again. I said that if using persuasion and influence scares you, you should stop reading. That’s because there aren’t enough pages in this book— nor is it my intention—to try to convince you of the morality of using a fear appeal. I mean, what could I possibly say to convince you that it’s okay to use fear when selling your brake pad replacement service? (Isn’t it obvious?) Or life insurance? Home smoke detectors? Cancer insurance? The mere mention of these things—to me, anyway—conjures up fearful situations that require some form of self-protection. If that form of self-protection presents itself via an advertiser who happens to be selling a product that can save my life, prevent pain, or otherwise help me better deal with an unpleasant situation, then I welcome it. I have no problem being informed, and swiftly moved to take caution. Do you? Bottom line: if it’s possible to use fear to effectively sell a product or service, it means that inherent in that product or service is the possible resolution to that which is feared. If not, no matter how much fear you try to conjure up, your appeal will fail miserably. Make sense? The Four-Step Recipe for Inducing Fear Okay, so you’ve determined that your product or service can genuinely alleviate a real fear-producing problem and is a good candidate for using the fear appeal. In order to make it work, there’s a specific, fouringredient recipe you must follow. In their study, Age of Propaganda (2001), Pratkanis and Aronson argue that, “the fear appeal is most effective when: 1. It scares the hell out of people. 2. It offers a specific recommendation for overcoming the fear-aroused threat. 3. The recommended action is perceived as effective for reducing the threat. 4. The message recipient believes that he or she can perform the recommended action.” CA$HVERTISING 32 The success or failure of this strategy relies on the existence of all four components. Remove any one of them, and it’s like building your own computer and leaving out the hard drive. No matter how much you want it to work, it simply won’t compute! What’s more, if you create too much fear, you could actually scare someone to inaction, like a deer, staring frozen into the headlights of an oncoming SUV. Fear can paralyze. And it will motivate your prospect to act only if he believes he has the power to change his situation. That means in order to craft an effective fear appeal, your ad must contain specific, believable recommendations for reducing the threat that are both credible and achievable. For example, let’s say you own a karate school and you’re selling self-defense training. You can teach people to walk even the roughest streets with the confidence of a trained bodyguard, ready to counter even the most vicious attacks by the scariest (and ugliest) thugs walking the earth. Fact is, you need to do more than simply present gruesome crime stats. You must also convince your prospect that it’s within her ability—using your system—to fight off an attacker using her bare hands. Ignore this vital step, and all you’ve accomplished is scaring her. You must also convince her, using factors that boost credibility (testimonials, video demonstrations, free lessons, and other believability boosters that we’ll discuss later), and open her mind to the possibility that your claim is true, and that she really can enjoy the benefits you’re promising. (She wants to believe you, because you’re making an appealing claim. It’s your job to help her believe you, and that takes more than simply shouting “boo!”) The fear appeal is also more successful if the fears targeted are specific and widely recognized. It’s a lot easier to sell your sunscreen because everyone knows the sun can fry you like bacon and turn your skin into a melanoma factory. It’s much tougher to sell laundry detergent that helps prevent ultraviolet damage to clothing. Why? Because few people are concerned with UV laundry damage. When’s the last time this issue kept you awake? Although the fear is specific (damage to clothing), it’s certainly not widely recognized. Listen: Your goal is not to create new fears, but to tap into existing fears, either those on the forefront of consumers’ minds, or those that require a little digging to uncover. For example, take what I affectionately call “germ gel.” You may know it as Purell Instant Hand Sanitizer, the leading brand. I don’t go How to Get Inside Their Heads 33 anywhere without it. In fact, if I leave the house and forget my small bottle, I’m thrown into somewhat of a panic. Why is this? GOJO Industries— the company that manufactures the germ-quashing goop—first introduced Purell to the food service and healthcare industries in 1988. Thinking back to that time—and even before—I don’t recall ever feeling creeped out about touching things in public the way I do today. Sure, I was always health conscious; I always washed my hands before eating, and throughout the day as needed. I knew germs existed everywhere. And yet, the “need” to keep my hands relatively germ-free was simply not a concern back then. It wasn’t on the forefront of my mind. Jump ahead to 1997, when Purell hit the consumer market. Aha! Did you know that unwashed hands are the leading cause of food contamination in restaurants? Hand-washing? What a joke! A 2003 survey sponsored by the American Society of Microbiology (ASM) found that many people passing through major U.S. airports don’t wash their hands after using the public facilities. More than 30 percent of people using restrooms in New York airports, 19 percent of those in Miami’s airport, and 27 percent of air travelers at Chicago’s O’Hare aren’t stopping to wash their hands. In a phone survey the same year conducted by Wirthlin Worldwide, only 58 percent of people say they wash their hands after sneezing or coughing, and only 77 percent say they wash their hands after changing a diaper. In 1972, the Journal of the American Medical Association described a study wherein they cultured bacteria from 200 coins and bills and found fecal bacteria and Staphylococcus aureus on 13 percent of coins and 42 percent of notes. It concluded: “Money is truly dirty.” Heck, visit Purell.com and you’ll see their list of “99.99 Germy Reasons to Use Purell.” Listerine created a shockwave of paranoia with the distasteful word halitosis in 1900. The copywriter for antiperspirant Odorno (what a name!) caused ladies to question their “daintiness” with a groundbreaking headline in the 1919 Ladies Home Journal that read, “In the Curve of a Woman’s Arm.” GOJO did the same for bacteria. They made it an issue. Something to think—and fret—about. They instilled fear. And, as a result, Listerine now boasts an impressive 53 percent market share. Odorno boosted sales 112 percent using that poetic headline (despite causing 200 women to cancel their subscriptions out of sheer disgust with the suggestion that they’d need such a product). And today, GOJO’s Purell is the largest-selling brand of instant hand sanitizer, causing countless CA$HVERTISING 34 germaphobes to carry the stuff around in their handy travel bottle holders that attach conveniently to their key chains. (See how they made it easy to resolve the fear?) A common way fear is used to simulate action is via the use of deadlines and scarcity. Phrases and slogans such as limited offer, one-day sale, and while supplies last have the effect of scaring consumers into believing that unless they act now, they’ll miss a fantastic opportunity to save money, tapping into Human Secondary Want #9. The deadline tactic follows the guidelines by offering the consumer the means to address the “threat” by rushing out to purchase before it’s too late. However, fear is not a magical wand. It’s not enough to simply scare someone, say a few nice things about your product, and sit back and wait for an onslaught of orders. Fear is simply one way to motivate your prospects to investigate your product further. Get it? You still need to convince him that your product provides the solution to the fear you just instilled. You still need to persuade and motivate him to take action: to grab his wallet, visit your Website, or call your 800 number and place his order. Don’t fret! I’ll teach you how to do all these things—and much more—in Chapter 3, where we discuss 41 advertising-specific techniques that incorporate many of the psychological principles we’re now reviewing. Principle #2: Ego Morphing— Instant Identification When you see the Marlboro man, it’s your ego—not your craving for paper tubes stuffed with tobacco—that motivates you to switch brands. When you see the Victoria’s Secret models with their long, silky hair and piercing eyes slinking around in their lacy undergarments, it’s your ego, not your admiration for the directorial style of the commercial, that motivates you to buy the slinkwear. The fact is, you can blame your ego for many of your high credit card bills. The foundation for Ego Morphing and the Vanity Appeal was described by Pratkanis and Aronson (Age of Propaganda, 1991), when they said, “By purchasing the ‘right stuff,’ we [the consumer] enhance our own egos and rationalize away our inadequacies.” Imagine that! We can actually buy things to make up for what we believe is a lacking in our personalities. You’ve heard of retail therapy, right? Could it be that we as advertisers are actually performing a How to Get Inside Their Heads 35 function more vital than simply providing people with goods and services? Could it be that we’re actually assisting in our customers’ psychological development as well? In reality, this technique allows you to create a certain image, or identity, for a product, in order to appeal to a particular section of the audience that feels that their personal image and ego either match it or could be improved by it. Your goal is to cause consumers to become so closely associated with the product’s image that it almost becomes a part of their own identity; thus, you’re “morphing” their ego to fit your product. By representing your product through carefully chosen images and personalities, you can persuade your prospects that, by purchasing or using your wares, they’ll immediately become associated with these images and attitudes. Persuading this way is not difficult. You don’t have to work hard to persuade a woman to want to be sexier and more in control, or for a man to be more powerful, self-confident, and appealing to women. These things are built in, pre-wired into our very being. And because the majority of true prospects for your product already believe they possess the ideas and values associated with it—or have the desire to develop them (otherwise they wouldn’t be true prospects)—you’re actually tapping into this pre-wiring. Don’t you see? You’re selling an easy route to fulfill what we know they already want more of. And for those who believe they already have it, our product can help them too, by giving them a way to express what they feel about themselves to the outside world. What does all this mean? Simply that you can appeal to your audience’s vanity and ego without the need for persuasive ideas or evidence by concentrating on showing your prospects the images they want to see. For example, start noticing how very little persuasive copy is used in ads for luxury goods. They’re “feel good” ads. They present an image that’s carefully crafted to evoke the emotional response of desire—for the item advertised. Here’s an example of the elaborate and complex purchase decision pattern when such an ad is viewed by a true prospect: “Oooooh, look at these hot-looking girls climbing all over that guy wearing those kewl Hollister jeans. I want those jeans.” Don’t laugh. That’s about it all it takes. And if it didn’t work, retailers such as Hollister and Abercrombie & Fitch wouldn’t be spending a fortune placing such ads. (Nor would Lexus, BMW, Jaguar, and CA$HVERTISING 36 high-end-product advertisers of most every kind. Oh, did I mention Rolls-Royce? Yeah, them too.) Does it work? Consider the perfume and cologne business. Aside from impregnating paper flaps with their product so people can take a whiff, the only thing these advertisers do to persuade their prospects to buy is show photos of hot-looking women and men whom we’re supposed to believe are customers. The models aren’t even wearing the perfumes and colognes during the photo shoot! So really, 99.9 percent of the ad has nothing to do with the products being promoted. It’s pure imagery. But manufacturers apparently know it works: 2008 cologne sales are expected to reach $1.6 billion. Women’s fragrances? Add another $3.2 billion. Appealing to people’s vanity and ego is most successful when it hones in on characteristics that society considers being desirable, such as physical attractiveness, intelligence, economic success, and sexual prowess. As suggested by Stec and Bernstein’s Balance Theory (1999), if consumers are presented with the “correct” images, people who possess these characteristics will buy them in order to publicize their ego. Those who don’t will purchase them in an attempt to appear as if they do. Interesting, isn’t it? So think about your product. Does owning or using it suggest qualities that people would want to flaunt? You own a karate school? Then spotlight the names of the big mixed martial arts stars who work out there. Then print and sell T-shirts that say “I train with [insert bigname star here].” Instant ego appeal. You’re the most expensive dog groomer in town? Show photos of the rich celebrities who bring in their pooches. Feature Mr. or Ms. Celeb stepping out of a limo with a drooling pooch. “Oh, yes...there are plenty of other groomers in town, but pshaw! I only trust the Karringtons with my Fluffy.” So snotty, but—BOOM!—instant ego appeal. You’re a printer specializing in high-end stationery and wedding invitations? Brag about the well-known personalities who’ve used your services. Huh? You say there are no well-known personalities who’ve used your services? That’s an easy fix. Offer to do a free job for a few of your favorite local celebs—newscasters, or social and political leaders, for example. When they accept, send them 250 letterheads and envelopes on your finest paper...then drop some names as to whose stationery you’ve printed. Voila! Instant ego appeal. Say, “Why Do More Local Bank Presidents Choose FortKnox Security to Protect Their Own Homes Than Anyone Else?” And then, the variation: “Why Do More Local Jewelry Store Owners Choose FortKnox Security to Protect Their Homes Than Anyone Else?” Get it? If bank presidents and jewelry store owners trust you to protect their family and their biggest investment (their home), then, as the average prospect, I’d feel good about hiring you to secure my modest home. Doing so puts me in the company of these discerning executives. Again, instant ego appeal. Back to Rolls-Royce.
